persons.note: APPOINTED THE TOWN'S FIRST STREET COMMISSIONER ON 7 NOVEMBER 1833 and resigned before his term expired: Andreas, 'It was during these days that Benjamin Jones was appointed Street Commissioner, but on account of ill-health resigned before his term expired, and was succeeded by O. Morrison and Silas W. Sherman.' His health is the only medical fact about any private resident in this parcel. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds; an advertiser in it was paying to be found, which makes it strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835, nineteen months and about 2,400 people later. OLD SETTLERS, 1882 — A DATE OF DEATH, AND NOTHING ABOUT 1835. John Wentworth's roll of old settlers who had died since 1 January 1881, kept for the Calumet Club and printed in the Chicago Tribune of 25 April 1882, carries “Benjamin Jones, Aug. 11, 1881.”. That corroborates a Chicago residence before 1840 and fixes the END of this life, which this record did not carry; it is not an arrival and it places nobody in the town on 1 July 1835. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 1 time: Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Jones, Benjamin” (poll_1834_060, line 229). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Jones' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 5 times, as “JONES BENJAMIN”, 1833-10-22 to 1836-06-22: 1 lot in the platted town — lot 7 of block 35 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L7BL35CHIOT, as printed) and 4 parcels of the school section — BL121 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; lot 2 of block 117 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 4 of block 23 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 4 of block 80 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $7133.00 (ls0254, ls0255, ls0256, ls0257, ls1263). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $6000.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: JONES BENJAMIN matches Benjamin Jones: the forename names Benjamin Jones of the 6 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

resident_research.summary: Independently corroborated. Benjamin Jones agrees, forename for forename or initial for initial, with a record outside the post-office lists in the town's 1833 tax and 1834/1835 poll lists, the Fergus 1839/1843 and Norris 1844 directories, the old-settler rolls and Fergus's death notices. one resident of the surname 'Jones' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered.
resident_research.notes: FERGUS 26-29, AS PRINTED: "Jones, Benj. (B. J. & Co.), res 109 Randolph, bet Clark and Dearborn [died, Manitowoc, Wis., August 11, 1881, aged 87]". The 1843 directory prints the name in the firm B. Jones & Co. with a death date and age that put birth about 1794. The surname is one of the town's commonest and the agreement is on the forename initial only, so the reading enriches without settling. Research only. Later-volume readings are recorded here and NOT promoted: T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply.

research_note: THE TOWN'S FIRST STREET COMMISSIONER, WHICH IS A JOB THIS DATASET'S GROUND LAYER SHOULD CARE ABOUT: the ordinances of 7 November 1833 that he was appointed to enforce are the same ones that document timber, stone, brick, boxes and barrels stacked in the streets and hogs running at large. He is the man who was supposed to stop it, and he was ill.
